loads.label: 4 kN/m
loads.ask: How do I find the resultant of a distributed load?

explain.say: Snow on a roof, books along a shelf, water pressing on a tank wall: these loads are spread out, not concentrated at a point. We call them distributed loads, measured in kilonewtons per metre. Here a 6 metre beam carries 4 kilonewtons per metre over its left half. How do we handle that?

loads.label: 4 kN/m
loads.ask: How do I find the resultant of a distributed load?

draw.text: Beam: 6 m span, 4 kN/m over the first 3 m

explain.say: Here is the trick: replace the whole spread-out load with one equivalent force. Its size is the area under the load diagram: 4 kilonewtons per metre times 3 metres, which is 12 kilonewtons. See the shaded load on the left? What would the area be for a triangle-shaped load?

loads.label: 4 kN/m
loads.ask: How do I find the resultant of a distributed load?

explain.say: Half base times height! And where does the 12 kilonewtons act? At the centroid of the load shape: for a rectangle, the middle, 1.5 metres from the left. For a triangle it would be a third of the way from the tall end. Now take moments about the left pin: the right reaction times 6 equals 12 times 1.5. What do you get?

loads.label: 4 kN/m
loads.ask: How do I find the resultant of a distributed load?

explain.say: Three kilonewtons. The left pin takes the rest, 12 minus 3, which is 9 kilonewtons. Look at the shear diagram: it falls steadily under the load and crosses zero at 2.25 metres. That is where the bending moment peaks. Why there?

loads.label: 4 kN/m
loads.ask: How do I find the resultant of a distributed load?

explain.say: Because the slope of the moment diagram is the shear, so zero shear means a peak. The maximum moment is 9 times 2.25 minus 4 times 2.25 squared over 2, which is about 10.1 kilonewton metres. See the curve? Great work! Warning: the resultant is fine for reactions, but never use it to draw shear inside the loaded length.

faq.q: How do I find the resultant of a distributed load?
faq.a: Its size equals the area under the load intensity diagram. For a uniform load that is the intensity times the loaded length; for a triangle it is half the base times the peak intensity.
asks: equivalent point load of distributed load

faq.q: Where does the resultant of a UDL act?
faq.a: At the centroid of the load diagram. For a uniform load that is the middle of the loaded length; for a triangular load it is one third of the length from the larger end.
asks: line of action of resultant distributed load

faq.q: How do I find the reactions of a beam with a partial UDL?
faq.a: Replace the load with its resultant at the centroid, take moments about one support for the other reaction, then use the vertical force sum for the first.

faq.q: Why is the maximum bending moment where shear is zero?
faq.a: The slope of the bending moment diagram equals the shear force. Where the shear crosses zero, the slope is zero, so the moment reaches a maximum or minimum.

faq.q: Can I use the resultant to draw the shear force diagram?
faq.a: Only outside the loaded region. Inside it, the shear changes steadily along the load, so you must use the actual distributed load, not one point force.
asks: when not to use equivalent load

facts: The resultant of a triangular distributed load acts one third of the span from its larger end.
The slope of a beam's bending moment diagram equals the shear force at that point.
